danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 2
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovnas salon fyldtes efterhånden. Det højeste selskab i Petersborg var samlet her: mennesker, der var vidt forskellige i alder og temperament, men som alle tilhørte den samme sociale verden. Fyrst Vasilijs datter, den smukke Hélène, var kommet for at hente sin far til ambassadørens fest; hun bar en balkjole og sit hofdamemærke. Den unge lille fyrstinde Bolkonskaja, kendt som den mest charmerende kvinde i Petersborg, var der også. Hun var blevet gift den foregående vinter, og da hun var gravid, kom hun ikke længere til store selskaber — kun til små sammenkomster. Fyrst Vasilijs søn Hippolyte var kommet med Mortemart, som han introducerede. Abbé Morio og mange andre var også mødt op.
* Den mest fascinerende kvinde i Petersborg.

Til hver ny gæst sagde Anna Pavlovna: »De har endnu ikke set min tante,« eller »De kender ikke min tante?« — og med stor højtidelighed førte hun hver enkelt hen til en lille gammel dame med store sløjfer af bånd i sin kappe, der var kommet sejlende ind fra et andet værelse, så snart gæsterne begyndte at ankomme. Anna Pavlovna drejede langsomt blikket fra den besøgende til sin tante, annoncerede hver persons navn og forlod dem derefter.

Hver gæst gennemgik ritualet med at hilse på denne gamle tante, som ingen af dem kendte, ingen af dem ønskede at kende, og ingen af dem brød sig om. Anna Pavlovna fulgte disse hilsner med sørgmodig, højtidelig interesse og tavs billigelse. Tanten sagde det samme til hver enkelt: hun spurgte til deres helbred og talte om sit eget, og om Hendes Majestæts helbred, som »Gud ske tak havde det bedre i dag.« Og hver gæst, selvom høfligheden hindrede dem i at vise utålmodighed, forlod den gamle kvinde med en følelse af lettelse over at have udført en irriterende forpligtelse, og nærmede sig hende ikke igen resten af aftenen.

Den unge fyrstinde Bolkonskaja havde medbragt håndarbejde i en guldbrocheret fløjlstaske. Hendes nydelige lille overlæbe, hvorpå en svag mørk dun lige kunne anes, var for kort til hendes tænder, men det fik den blot til at krølle sig endnu sødere opad og var særlig charmerende, når hun af og til trak den ned for at møde underlæben. Som det altid er tilfældet med en virkelig tiltrækkende kvinde, syntes hendes fejl — den korte overlæbe og den halvåbne mund — at være hendes egen unikke og særlige form for skønhed. Alle lyste op ved synet af denne smukke unge kvinde, der så snart skulle blive mor, så fuld af liv og sundhed, og som bar sin byrde så let. Gamle mænd og kedede, modløse unge, der tilbragte tid i hendes selskab og talte med hende, følte, at de selv også blev fyldt af liv og energi, ligesom hende. Alle der talte med hende og ved hvert ord så hendes lyse smil og det stadige glimt af hendes hvide tænder, troede, at de var i særlig godt humør den dag.

Den lille fyrstinde gik rundt om bordet med hurtige, korte, vuggende skridt, håndarbejdstasken over armen, og bredte muntert sin kjole ud og satte sig i en sofa nær sølvsamovaren, som om alt, hvad hun foretog sig, var en fornøjelse for hende selv og alle omkring hende. [På fransk] »Jeg har taget mit arbejde med,« sagde hun og viste sin taske til hele selskabet. [På fransk] »Pas nu på, Annette, jeg håber ikke, De har spillet mig et puds,« tilføjede hun og vendte sig mod sin værtinde. [På fransk] »De skrev, at det bare ville være en lille sammenkomst — og se, hvor dårligt jeg er klædt på.« Og hun bredte armene vidt ud for at vise sin kortlivede, blondekantede, elegante grå kjole, strammet med et bredt bånd lige under brystet.
[På fransk] »Vær ikke bekymret, Lise — De vil altid være smukkere end alle andre,« svarede Anna Pavlovna.

[På fransk] »Ved De,« sagde fyrstinden i samme tonefald, stadig på fransk, idet hun vendte sig mod en general, »min mand forlader mig? Han tager af sted for at lade sig slå ihjel. Sig mig — hvad er denne forfærdelige krig overhovedet for?« tilføjede hun og vendte sig mod fyrst Vasilij, og uden at vente på svar henvendte hun sig til hans datter, den smukke Hélène.
»Hvilken dejlig kvinde, denne lille fyrstinde!« sagde fyrst Vasilij til Anna Pavlovna.

En af de næste gæster, der ankom, var en svær ung mand med kortklippet hår, briller og de lyse bukser, der var moderne på den tid. Han bar et meget højt halskraveflæse og en brun kjolefrakke. Denne fyldige unge mand var den uægte søn af grev Bezukhov, en velkendt stormand fra Katarina den Stores tid, som nu lå for døden i Moskva. Den unge mand havde endnu ikke trådt ind i hverken militær- eller statstjenesten, da han lige var vendt hjem fra udlandet, hvor han var blevet uddannet; dette var hans første optræden i selskabslivet. Anna Pavlovna modtog ham med det minimale nik, hun reserverede til det laveste trin i sin salons hierarki. Men trods denne kolde velkomst gled et udtryk af uro og alarm over hendes ansigt, da hun så Pierre (Pjotr Bezukhov) komme ind — som om noget for stort og upassende til rummet var dukket op. Og selvom han ganske vist var større end de andre tilstedeværende mænd, kunne hendes uro kun stamme fra det kloge og dog sky, opmærksomme og dog naturlige udtryk, der adskilte ham fra alle andre i salen.
[På fransk] »Det er så venligt af Dem, monsieur Pierre, at komme og besøge en stakkels syg kvinde,« sagde Anna Pavlovna og udvekslede et uroligt blik med sin tante, mens hun førte ham derhen.
Pierre mumlede noget uhørligt og blev ved med at se sig omkring, som om han ledte efter noget. På vej hen til tanten smilede han varmt til den lille fyrstinde, som man gør til en nær bekendt.

Anna Pavlovnas uro viste sig berettiget, for Pierre vendte sig fra tanten uden at vente på at høre hendes bemærkninger om Hendes Majestæts helbred. Anna Pavlovna greb ham i forfærdelse og sagde: »Kender De abbé Morio? Han er en yderst interessant mand.«
»Ja, jeg har hørt om hans plan for evig fred, og den er meget interessant — men næppe praktisk.«

»Mener De det?« sagde Anna Pavlovna, der gerne ville sige noget, før hun slap fri for at passe sine pligter som værtinde. Men Pierre begik nu sin anden sociale brøler. Først havde han forladt en dame, før hun var færdig med at tale til ham; nu fortsatte han med at tale til en person, der tydeligvis ville slippe væk. Med hovedet bøjet fremad og sine store fødder bredt plantet fra hinanden kastede han sig ud i en forklaring af, hvorfor han anså abbéens plan for urealistisk.
»Vi taler om det senere,« sagde Anna Pavlovna med et smil.

Da hun havde befriet sig fra denne unge mand, der ikke forstod at opføre sig, vendte hun tilbage til sine pligter som værtinde og fortsatte med at observere og lytte, klar til at træde til, hvor samtalen kunne gå i stå. Som formanden i en spinderi, der efter at have sat arbejderne i gang går rundt og lægger mærke til, hvor en ten er gået i stå, eller hvor en knirker eller larmer for meget, og skynder sig hen for at bremse den eller få den til at køre rigtigt — sådan bevægede Anna Pavlovna sig gennem sin salon, nærmede sig først en gruppe, der var gået i stå, så en, der var blevet for højlydt, og med et ord her og en lille justering dér holdt hun samtalemaskineriet kørende jævnt og støt. Men gennem alt dette var hendes uro over Pierre tydelig. Hun iagttog nervøst, når han gled hen mod gruppen omkring Mortemart for at lytte med, og igen, når han bevægede sig videre til kredsen samlet omkring abbéen.

Pierre var blevet uddannet i udlandet, og denne aften hos Anna Pavlovna var det første selskab, han deltog i i Rusland. Han vidste, at alle Petersborgs intellektuelle stjerner var samlet her, og som et barn i en legetøjsbutik vidste han ikke, hvor han skulle kigge hen, bange for at gå glip af en eller anden brilliant samtale. Da han så de selvsikre, polerede udtryk i ansigterne omkring sig, ventede han hele tiden at høre noget virkelig dybtgående. Til sidst fandt han vej hen til Morio. Samtalen dér virkede interessant, og han stod og ventede på en chance for at dele sine egne synspunkter, som unge mennesker altid gør.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's drawing room was gradually filling up. The highest society of Petersburg was gathered there: people who differed widely in age and temperament but who all belonged to the same social world. Prince Vasili's daughter, the beautiful Hélène, came to collect her father for the ambassador's party; she wore a ball gown and her badge as lady-in-waiting. The youthful little Princess Bolkonskaya, known as the most captivating woman in Petersburg, was also there. She had married the previous winter and, being pregnant, no longer attended large gatherings — only small receptions. Prince Vasili's son Hippolyte had arrived with Mortemart, whom he introduced. The Abbé Morio and many others had come as well.
* The most fascinating woman in Petersburg.

To each new guest Anna Pavlovna said, "You haven't yet seen my aunt," or "You don't know my aunt?" — and with great solemnity she escorted each one over to a little old lady wearing large ribbon bows in her cap, who had come sailing in from another room as soon as the guests began arriving. Slowly turning her eyes from the visitor to her aunt, Anna Pavlovna would announce each person's name and then leave them.

Every guest went through the ritual of greeting this old aunt whom none of them knew, none of them wanted to know, and none of them cared about. Anna Pavlovna watched these greetings with mournful, solemn interest and silent approval. The aunt said the same thing to each of them: she asked about their health and spoke of her own, and about the health of Her Majesty, who "thank God, was feeling better today." And each guest, though politeness prevented them from showing impatience, left the old woman with a sense of relief at having performed an annoying obligation, and did not go near her again for the rest of the evening.

The young Princess Bolkonskaya had brought some needlework in a gold-embroidered velvet bag. Her pretty little upper lip, on which a faint dark down was just visible, was too short for her teeth, but this only made it curl up more sweetly, and was especially charming when she sometimes drew it down to meet her lower lip. As is always the case with a truly attractive woman, her flaw — the shortness of her upper lip and her half-open mouth — seemed to be her own unique and special form of beauty. Everyone brightened at the sight of this pretty young woman, so soon to be a mother, so full of life and health, carrying her burden so lightly. Old men and bored, dispirited young ones who spent time in her company and talked with her felt as though they too were becoming, like her, full of life and energy. Everyone who spoke with her, watching at each word her bright smile and the constant gleam of her white teeth, thought themselves to be in an especially good mood that day.

The little princess circled the table with quick, short, swaying steps, her workbag on her arm, and cheerfully spreading out her skirts, sat down on a sofa near the silver samovar as though everything she did was a pleasure to herself and to everyone around her. [Speaking in French] "I've brought my work," she said, showing her bag and addressing the whole room. [Speaking in French] "Mind you, Annette, I hope you haven't played a trick on me," she added, turning to her hostess. [Speaking in French] "You wrote that it would be just a small gathering — and look how badly I'm dressed." And she spread her arms wide to show off her short-waisted, lace-trimmed, elegant gray dress, cinched with a broad ribbon just below the bust.
[Speaking in French] "Don't worry, Lise — you will always be prettier than anyone else," replied Anna Pavlovna.

[Speaking in French] "You know," said the princess in the same tone of voice, still in French, turning to a general, "my husband is abandoning me? He's going off to get himself killed. Tell me — what is this awful war even for?" she added, turning to Prince Vasili, and without waiting for an answer she turned to speak to his daughter, the beautiful Hélène.
"What a delightful woman this little princess is!" said Prince Vasili to Anna Pavlovna.

One of the next guests to arrive was a heavyset young man with close-cropped hair, spectacles, and the light-colored trousers that were fashionable at the time. He wore a very high collar ruffle and a brown dress coat. This stout young man was the illegitimate son of Count Bezukhov, a well-known grandee from Catherine the Great's era, who was now lying on his deathbed in Moscow. The young man had not yet entered either the military or the civil service, having only just returned from abroad where he had been educated; this was his first appearance in society. Anna Pavlovna greeted him with the minimal nod she reserved for the lowest tier of her drawing room hierarchy. But despite this cold welcome, a look of anxiety and alarm crossed her face when she saw Pierre enter — as though something too large and unsuited to the room had appeared. And although he was certainly bigger than the other men present, her unease could only have stemmed from the clever yet shy, observant yet natural expression that set him apart from everyone else in that drawing room.
[Speaking in French] "It is so good of you, Monsieur Pierre, to come visit a poor invalid," said Anna Pavlovna, exchanging an anxious look with her aunt as she led him over.
Pierre mumbled something inaudible and kept looking around as though searching for something. On his way to the aunt, he smiled warmly at the little princess, as one does to a close acquaintance.

Anna Pavlovna's alarm proved justified, for Pierre turned away from the aunt without waiting to hear her remarks about Her Majesty's health. Anna Pavlovna caught him in dismay and said, "Do you know the Abbé Morio? He is a most interesting man."
"Yes, I've heard about his plan for perpetual peace, and it's very interesting — but hardly practical."

"You think so?" said Anna Pavlovna, wanting to say something before escaping to attend to her duties as hostess. But Pierre now committed a second social blunder. First he had walked away from a lady before she finished speaking to him; now he continued talking to someone who clearly wanted to get away. With his head bent forward and his big feet planted wide apart, he launched into an explanation of why he considered the abbé's plan unrealistic.
"We'll discuss it later," said Anna Pavlovna with a smile.

Having rid herself of this young man who didn't know how to behave, she went back to her duties as hostess, continuing to observe and listen, ready to step in wherever the conversation might stall. Like the foreman in a spinning mill who, after setting the workers to their tasks, walks around noticing where a spindle has stopped or where one is creaking or making too much noise, and hurries to slow it down or get it running properly — so Anna Pavlovna moved through her drawing room, approaching first a group that had gone quiet, then one that had grown too loud, and with a word here or a slight adjustment there, she kept the conversational machine running smoothly and steadily. But through all of this, her anxiety about Pierre was obvious. She watched nervously whenever he drifted near the group around Mortemart to listen in, and again when he moved on to the circle gathered around the abbé.

Pierre had been educated abroad, and this evening at Anna Pavlovna's was the first society reception he had attended in Russia. He knew that all the intellectual stars of Petersburg were gathered here, and like a child in a toy shop, he didn't know which way to look, afraid of missing some brilliant conversation. Seeing the self-assured, polished expressions on the faces around him, he kept expecting to hear something truly profound. At last he made his way over to Morio. The conversation there seemed interesting, and he stood waiting for a chance to share his own views, the way young people always do.
